text: Welcome to your bistro! Your first dish will be {recipe}. You need at least {requirements}. Explore the stores and shelves, then drag packages into your cart. You may buy extras, but checkout must be affordable and leave you enough ingredients for this dish. Open the cart to remove packages. Pantry and Menu remain available.

Before cooking, sort the new foods into Green, Yellow or Red. These are the game's Traffic Light groups: Green is the everyday foundation, Yellow is for moderation, and Red is for occasional choices. Flip cards to inspect ingredients. Correct answers earn a refund on this checkout: higher accuracy gives a larger refund, and all correct earns up to {maxDiscount} back. You can rearrange cards before submitting. There is no retry after submission; a wrong food can return on a later purchase.
Let's cook the ingredients you prepared. Choose {recipe} for this first lesson. Other recipes will be available after the lesson. You can still inspect your pantry or return to the main menu.

Drag one serving at a time into the recipe slots for {recipe}. Required slots need the exact category and count. Optional slots may stay empty, or be filled exactly. A red rim means something needs attention. Open a slot to drag a serving back out. Review the dish whenever you like; this first lesson requires a successful recipe before you can confirm serving.

Your first recipe is built! You used {ingredients}. This dish changed health by {healthDelta} and covered these Daily Dozen groups: {dailyDozen}. In this game, Green servings and the Daily Dozen groups they cover contribute to health. Different groups add variety; repeating the same group does not add another coverage bonus. Positive health gains per dish are capped. Aim for variety within the recipe's slots, rather than piling on extra servings. From now on, you may also serve imperfect recipes and face their consequences.

You have now heard both sides of a rush and crash. A brief lift can feel encouraging, yet it may not last. Watch the customer's experience over time. Here, rush/crash is visual and dialogue feedback: it adds no extra health penalty beyond the dish's normal calculation. Think about the ingredients and the overall meal, rather than treating a burst of energy as proof of a good result.
